extracted.intended_audience: researchers and students interested in automatic theorem proving (prospective PhD students/postdocs, mathematicians and computer scientists)
extracted.subtask_description: Announcement and statement of aims for a GOFAI-style research project in automatic theorem proving, describing the project's goals, desired outputs, candidate qualities, organisation, and norms for acceptable methods. Intended to guide applicants and collaborators and set expectations for the project's direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for GOFAI approach / enthusiasm for GOFAI
rubrics_metrics.description: The most important quality I am looking for in an applicant ... is a genuine enthusiasm for the GOFAI approach briefly outlined here and explained in more detail in the much longer document.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants should read the longer 54-page document to understand the aims and approach; if you are drawn into thinking about the problems raised there, that's a very good sign. If your instinctive reaction is that the proposed GOFAI approach is the wrong way and that other techniques (e.g. machine learning, large search) should be used instead, the project probably isn’t a good fit for you.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not primarily a machine-learning project (expectation-setting)
rubrics_metrics.description: The project I am starting will not be a machine-learning project ... I would welcome and even expect collaboration with machine-learning researchers, but the core is GOFAI, not ML.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The announcement clarifies boundaries so applicants don't have an incorrect picture of the work. ML techniques may be used in combination (e.g. to choose among a small set of GOFAI-generated options), but machine learning should not be the main paradigm for the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of large brute-force searches / discourage 'silly' searches
rubrics_metrics.description: I will not be satisfied with programs that find proofs after carrying out large searches, even if those searches are small enough to be feasible. More precisely, searches will be strongly discouraged unless human mathematicians would also need to do them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowing a program to carry out searches of 'silly' options that humans would never do is running away from this absolutely central question. The project focuses on methods that mirror how humans prune search trees rather than brute-force tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human-like proof-finding with minimal backtracking
rubrics_metrics.description: Humans seem to be able to find proofs with a remarkably small amount of backtracking. How do they prune the search tree to such an extent?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms should imitate how humans find proofs and match human patterns of low backtracking; success is measured not only by whether a proof is found but by whether it was found in a way that resembles human reasoning (small backtracking, plausible heuristic moves).

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce proofs that are explainable/readable to humans
rubrics_metrics.description: Even a program that could solve only fairly easy problems but in a sufficiently human way that it could explain how it came up with its proofs could be a very valuable educational tool.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasis on human-comprehensible output: proofs should be presented so humans can follow the reasoning and see why steps are natural. 'Justified proof' / 'explicitly motivated proof' concepts are highlighted as desirable outputs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness at undergraduate level as a milestone
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t think it unreasonable to hope that within a few years there could be theorem-proving programs that were genuinely useful — not necessarily at a research level but at least at the level of a first-year undergraduate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measuring success includes practical usefulness even if limited to easier problems; the focus includes educational utility where the program helps learners understand proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of theoretical and practical work
rubrics_metrics.description: I don’t have strong views about the right balance between the theoretical and practical sides of the project, but I do feel strongly that both sides should be major components of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project outputs should include both theoretical advances (e.g., definitions like 'proof justification') and practical algorithm designs and implementations that inform each other.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open-source software and public reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: My plan at this stage is that any software associated with the project will be open source ... part of the plan is to report regularly and publicly on what we are thinking about, what problems ... are holding us up, and what progress we make.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Software and project reports should be made openly available to facilitate collaboration, reuse, and community contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for mathematical problem-solving experience over programming skill
rubrics_metrics.description: I think the ideal candidate is somebody with plenty of experience of solving mathematical problems ... and good programming ability. But if I had to choose one of the two, I would pick the former over the latter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates should demonstrate deep understanding of mathematical problem-solving; good programming skill is valuable but secondary if the candidate can convincingly specify implementable algorithms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Desire for detailed algorithm designs (implementable specifications)
rubrics_metrics.description: Part of the reason for that is that I hope that if one of the outputs of the group is detailed algorithm designs, then there will be remote participants who would enjoy turning those designs into code.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Algorithms should be specified clearly enough that others (possibly remote and not core team members) can implement them; design clarity and implementability are evaluation criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repository/database of 'justified' or 'motivated' proofs and accounts of idea origins
rubrics_metrics.description: I would love it if there were a large collection of such accounts, and I have it in mind as a possible idea to set up (with help) a repository for them ... One of the difficulties is that whereas there is widespread agreement about what constitutes a proof, there is not such a clear consensus about what constitutes a convincing explanation of where an idea comes from.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The repository should store proofs together with narratives/accounts explaining how the idea arose, aiming to capture 'proof justification' or 'explicitly motivated proof'; this may include multiple proofs, different hint sets, and stories of generation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reproducibility of proof-generation runs and experimental records
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s also desirable for the proofs to be 'reproducible' — that is, if the 'prover runs' which lead to those proofs can be reconstructed precisely later (by recording their exact inputs, including hint sets used, other parameters, and exact version of the prover itself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record exact inputs, hint sets, parameters, and software versions so experiments can be re-run and statistically analysed; this enables objective discussion of whether particular hints are 'cheating' or useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Store multiple proofs and failed attempts (database content and openness)
rubrics_metrics.description: The database of all 'motivated proofs' ought to include the ones in which the entire proof failed, though only some readers will want to see those in search results. Strictly speaking, it’s a database of 'motivated proof attempts', some successful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include successful and failed attempts, modular/hierarchical proof structures, and 'failure outputs' that explain why attempts failed to support learning and debugging of provers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design proofs and hints so they can be compared and evaluated empirically
rubrics_metrics.description: The database ... can include multiple proofs of the same theorem, in which different sets of hints were used, so their effect can be compared. Then instead of arguing about whether use of some hint is 'cheating' ... we can discuss whether it helps many problems or only a few, whether it slows down other problems, whether it can be effectively replaced with other hints which are more primitive or general, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation should be empirical: compare effects of hint-sets across problem sets, assess generality, trade-offs, and whether hints are 'human' or 'superhuman' by their effect and usage patterns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Team organisation expectations (frequency and purpose of meetings)
rubrics_metrics.description: I imagine something like twice a week for at least two hours and possibly more ... The purpose of the meetings will be to keep the project appropriately focused ... (i) to share ideas frequently, (ii) to keep thinking strategically ... and (iii) to keep updating our public list of open questions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Core group should operate as a genuine team (frequent scheduled meetings, sharing ideas, strategic planning, and maintaining an updated public list of open project questions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remote participation and community design (inclusiveness/moderation)
rubrics_metrics.description: I plan to work in as open a way as possible ... part of the plan is to report regularly and publicly ... I have not yet decided on the details of how remote participation might work. Maybe part of it could be fully open in the way that Polymath was, but part of it could be more private and carefully moderated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design participation modes to avoid excluding people (offer moderated/private spaces or separate groups communicating with the Cambridge core) and consider accessibility and safety concerns for historically marginalized groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow limited, well-scoped role types (e.g., remote implementers, admins)
rubrics_metrics.description: I could take on up to about three PhD students and two postdocs ... part of the plan is to report regularly and publicly ... if people want to use ideas generated by the project to incorporate into their own theorem-proving programs, I will very much welcome that.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Project roles can include core team researchers, remote participants who implement designs, administrators/web maintainers, and observers; contributions other than core research (e.g., admin help) are welcome.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptable integration of machine learning as a helper, not replacement
rubrics_metrics.description: I think there is plenty of potential for combining machine learning with GOFAI ideas — for example, one might use GOFAI to reduce the options for what the computer will do next to a small set and use machine learning to choose the option out of that small set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If ML is used, it should be integrated in a way that complements GOFAI principles (e.g., selection among human-style options), rather than replacing the human-like structuring of proof search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value placed on explanations of why proofs are natural (definition of success)
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are not fully satisfied with a proof unless you can see why it was natural for somebody to think of it, then that is better still.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful proof output should not only be correct but carry a convincing account of naturalness or justification for the key idea; the project cares about producing 'convincing explanations of where an idea comes from'.
